reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: A disorder of sex development in which a 46,XY individual with functioning testes cannot respond normally to androgens because of an androgen receptor defect
In the complete form, external genitalia are female, and the condition may present as primary amenorrhoea or as inguinal or labial masses (testes) in an otherwise typical-appearing girl
The partial form produces a spectrum of undervirilised or ambiguous genitalia depending on the degree of residual receptor function
Testes produce anti-Mullerian hormone, so Mullerian structures (uterus, upper vagina, fallopian tubes) are absent, but wolffian development is also impaired by androgen resistance
Biochemically, testosterone is in the normal or high male range with elevated LH, reflecting androgen resistance at the receptor rather than a synthetic defect
Breast development at puberty occurs through peripheral aromatisation of testosterone to oestrogen despite the absence of androgen action
Undescended testes carry a risk of malignancy that increases with age, informing decisions about the timing of gonadectomy
Care is best delivered by a multidisciplinary team addressing hormone replacement, psychological support, and sensitive discussion of gender identity and fertility
reference.pathophysiology: Androgen insensitivity syndrome results from mutations in the X-linked androgen receptor gene that impair the receptor's ability to bind androgen or transduce its signal. Although the testes of a 46,XY individual produce normal or elevated testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, target tissues cannot respond, so male external genital development and other androgen-dependent processes fail to varying degrees. Anti-Mullerian hormone from Sertoli cells still causes regression of Mullerian structures, so no uterus develops. Impaired negative feedback of androgens on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis raises LH, further increasing testosterone, part of which is aromatised peripherally to oestrogen, driving breast development at puberty. The severity of undervirilisation correlates with the degree of receptor dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causing genital ambiguity
additionalInvestigations: Anti-Mullerian hormone and assessment of internal Mullerian structures by imaging
Pelvic and inguinal imaging to locate gonads
Androgen receptor gene analysis to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling
Bone density assessment given long-term implications of hormone status and gonadectomy
redFlags: Malignant transformation of intra-abdominal or undescended testes, an increasing risk over time
Inguinal hernia or labial mass in a phenotypic girl warranting evaluation for gonads
Post-gonadectomy hypogonadism with accelerated bone loss if hormone replacement is inadequate
Significant psychological distress requiring timely support
reference.prognosis: With appropriate hormone replacement, gonadal management, and multidisciplinary support, individuals generally have good physical health and quality of life; the main long-term concerns are gonadal malignancy risk, bone health after gonadectomy, and psychosocial wellbeing. Fertility is not possible in the complete form.
pitfalls: Assuming a phenotypic female with primary amenorrhoea has a uterus without imaging
Overlooking androgen insensitivity in a girl presenting with inguinal or labial gonads
Neglecting oestrogen replacement and bone protection after gonadectomy
Communicating the diagnosis insensitively without multidisciplinary and psychological support
Confusing it with 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which has a different hormonal profile and pubertal course
management: Individualised gonadal management, with gonadectomy timing balanced against germ-cell malignancy risk and the option to retain gonads until after spontaneous puberty in complete cases
Oestrogen replacement therapy after gonadectomy to induce or maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone
Graduated vaginal dilation as first-line for vaginal hypoplasia in complete androgen insensitivity, with surgical vaginoplasty reserved for selected cases
In partial forms, sex-of-rearing and any genital surgery decisions individualised to phenotype and, where possible, the person's own gender identity
Bone-density surveillance with calcium and vitamin D optimisation given hypogonadism and post-gonadectomy fracture risk
Psychological support and care coordinated through a specialist disorders-of-sex-development multidisciplinary team
Genetic counselling for the X-linked androgen receptor mutation with testing of at-risk maternal-line relatives
